The reasoning is based on stereotypes about academic expectations. Typically, people tend to assume that children of physicians face higher academic pressure and are expected to earn top grades, so earning only a B might be viewed as disappointing. In contrast, the child of a cashier might be presumed to have lower expectations. Thus, even though both got a B, the cashier’s child (Ahmed Qureshi) likely felt relieved or pleasantly surprised by his grade because it was higher than what might have been expected for him.

The idea behind the puzzle is to compare expectations. Sam’s pharmacist parent might be expected to stress academic achievement—so Sam may not feel relieved for only getting a B—while Darnell, whose parent is a bartender, might not usually be pushed academically and therefore was pleasantly surprised (or "relieved") to get a B.

In contrast, the scientist’s child (Sam Zhang) might have faced higher expectations. Thus, Alex was the one who felt relieved that his grade was actually higher than he’d anticipated.

The reasoning is based on the common—the though stereotypical—expectation that an Asian student in a family of chemists is more likely to be held to very high academic standards (often expecting or typically earning A’s), while a Caucasian student from a similar family might not have the same high-pressure expectations. Thus, when both received a B in math, the Caucasian teenager would likely be relieved by receiving a higher grade than he was expecting, whereas the Asian teenager—who might have been aiming for an A—wouldn’t share that relief.
